title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 71
paragraphs: The burial-place of the kings is in the land of the Gerrians, the point up to which the Borysthenes is navigable. In this place, when their king has died, they make a large square excavation in the earth; and when it is ready, they take up the corpse (the body having been covered over with wax, the belly ripped open and cleansed and then sewn together again after being filled with cut-up galingale, spices, parsley-seed, and anise), and they convey it in a wagon to another nation. Those who receive the corpse thus conveyed to them do the same as the Royal Scythians: they cut off part of their ear, shave their hair round about, cut themselves all over the arms, tear at their forehead and nose, and pass arrows through their left hand. From there they convey the corpse of the king in the wagon to another of the nations over whom they rule; and those to whom they had first come accompany them. When they have gone round to all, conveying the corpse, they are in the land of the Gerrians, who have their settlements furthest away of all the nations over whom they rule, and they have reached the spot where the burial place is. After this, having placed the corpse in the tomb upon a bed of leaves, they stick spears along either side of the corpse, stretch pieces of wood across them, and cover the space with matting. Then they strangle and bury in the remaining space of the tomb one of the king's concubines, his cup-bearer, his cook, his groom, his attendant, and his messenger, along with horses, a first portion of everything else, and cups of gold (for silver they do not use at all, nor yet bronze). Having done this, they all join together to pile up a great mound, vying with one another and zealously trying to make it as large as possible.
